Introduction
We are sharing some extra reading materials with you. These are bonus topics that go beyond what we normally teach in class. The main purpose of these notes is to
give you additional knowledge that is usually learned after working in the industry for 1–2 years. By going through these materials, you can build a stronger
foundation and get a sense of what real-world developers deal with.
Please remember, these are not part of our regular syllabus. We will not be teaching or explaining these topics in class. They are only for your own exploration and
self-learning.
These bonus notes are meant to help you grow beyond the basics. If you learn them and mention these topics in your resume, it will give you an advantage while
searching for your job. Recruiters will notice that you have explored advanced concepts, which can make you stand out from others.
Treat these as an opportunity and not a requirement. Use them when you have time, once you are comfortable with the main course content.

We are sharing some extra reading materials with you. These are bonus topics that go beyond what we normally teach in class. The main purpose of these notes is to
give you additional knowledge that is usually learned after working in the industry for 1–2 years. By going through these materials, you can build a stronger
foundation and get a sense of what real-world developers deal with.
Please remember, these are not part of our regular syllabus. We will not be teaching or explaining these topics in class. They are only for your own exploration and
self-learning.
These bonus notes are meant to help you grow beyond the basics. If you learn them and mention these topics in your resume, it will give you an advantage while
searching for your job. Recruiters will notice that you have explored advanced concepts, which can make you stand out from others.
Treat these as an opportunity and not a requirement. Use them when you have time, once you are comfortable with the main course content.
MVC vs MVT
Model: Handles the data and database part.
View: Deals with how things look (UI).
Controller: Connects the model and view, controls the flow of data.
For example, if a user fills a login form: The Controller checks the request, the Model gets the user details from the database, and the View shows the result such as
login success or an error message.
Model: Manages data and database.
View: Contains the business logic (like a controller in MVC).
Template: Handles the presentation (HTML, CSS, UI).
For example, in Django, when you make a login page: The View function checks the request and logic, the Model talks to the database, and the Template shows the final
HTML page to the user.
Difference Between MVC and MVT
The difference between MVC and MVT lies in how they handle logic and presentation.
In MVC, the Controller is a separate component that manages the application logic, while in MVT, the View takes care of the logic. In MVC, the View manages
presentation, whereas in MVT, the Template handles presentation. MVC is used in many frameworks like Spring, ASP.NET, and Ruby on Rails, while MVT is mainly used in
Django.
Virtual Environment
The MVC pattern stands for Model – View – Controller. It is a common design pattern used in web development to organize code.
The MVT pattern stands for Model – View – Template. It is very similar to MVC, but commonly used in Django (a Python framework).
A virtual environment is an isolated space where you can install Python packages separately for each project. It helps manage dependencies
without affecting your system-wide Python installation.
In simple words, a virtual environment allows you to create a separate area on your computer where your project’s Python packages and dependencies are installed.
This way, different projects don’t interfere with each other, and you can use different versions of packages as needed.
We use a virtual environment in Django projects to keep project dependencies separate and organized, avoiding version conflicts and making the project portable.
Imagine working on multiple Django projects, and one needs Django version 3.2 while another needs Django version 4.2. Without a virtual environment, installing
one version will override the other. A virtual environment keeps them isolated so they don’t conflict.
How to Create a Virtual Environment?
First, we install the virtualenv tool using pip. Then, we create a virtual environment by running virtualenv venv. The folder venv will contain the isolated Python
environment. Finally, we activate the virtual environment:
On Windows, run venv\Scripts\activate.
On macOS/Linux, run source venv/bin/activate.
Once activated, any Python packages we install will stay inside this environment.
How to Deactivate a Virtual Environment?
After finishing work in the virtual environment, type deactivate to exit it. This returns you to the system’s normal Python environment.
How to Install Django in the Virtual Environment?
Once the virtual environment is activated, we use pip install django to install Django only inside this environment. This keeps your system clean and ensures
each project uses only the required dependencies.
Class-Based Views (CBVs)
In Django, views control what is displayed when a user visits a web page. Instead of writing functions for each view, CBVs let you use classes, which help organize
your code better by grouping related functionality.
Example:
# Step 1: Install virtualenv (only once)
pip install virtualenv
# Step 2: Create a virtual environment named 'venv'
virtualenv venv
# Step 3: Activate the virtual environment
# On Windows:
venv\Scripts\activate
# On macOS or Linux:
source venv/bin/activate
COPY
deactivate

pip install django

Class-Based Views (CBVs) in Django are views implemented as Python classes instead of functions. They provide an object-oriented way to build
views, making code more reusable and organized.
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.views import View
class HelloWorldView(View):
def get(self, request):
return HttpResponse("Hello, World!")
COPY
We import View from django.views. We create a class called HelloWorldView that inherits from View. Inside the class, we define a method called get that runs when
the user visits the page via an HTTP GET request. The view responds with "Hello, World!" as an HTTP response.
Generic Views
Instead of writing all the code from scratch, Django offers generic views that already do common jobs like showing a list of database records or a form for creating a
new record. You just configure them by telling what model or form to use.
Example:
We import ListView from django.views.generic. We create a class ProductListView that inherits from ListView. We specify the model as Product so that Django
knows which data to display. We tell Django to use the template product_list.html to show the list of products. Without writing code to fetch data or render the
template, Django does it automatically.
Mixins
Mixins help developers avoid repeating code. Instead of writing the same functionality in multiple views, you can create a mixin and include it in any view that needs
it. They are combined with other classes to extend behavior.
Example:
The GreetingMixin class defines one method, get_greeting(), which returns a message.
The MyView class inherits from both GreetingMixin and Django’s View.
The get() method calls get_greeting() from the mixin when a GET request is made.
The view returns the greeting message as an HttpResponse.
Hosting Django Application on Vercel
Vercel makes it simple to put your web project online. Even though it is mainly designed for frontend frameworks like Next.js, you can configure Django to work by
setting it up properly, so your web app runs from the cloud without managing your own server.
Example:
Generic Views in Django are pre-built, reusable views provided by Django that handle common tasks such as displaying a list of items, showing a
detail page, creating or updating records, etc (CRUD operations).
from django.views.generic import ListView
from .models import Product
class ProductListView(ListView):
model = Product
template_name = 'product_list.html'
COPY
A Mixin in Django is a type of class that provides reusable methods for other classes without being a complete class on its own. Mixins are often
used with Django’s class-based views to add extra functionality.
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.views import View
# Define a mixin
class GreetingMixin:
def get_greeting(self):
return "Hello, welcome to Django Mixins!"
# Use the mixin with a class-based view

Vercel is a cloud platform that allows developers to easily deploy web applications. It is commonly used for hosting frontend applications but can
also host Django applications using serverless functions or special configurations.
Install Vercel CLI:
Add a vercel.json file in your Django project root:
Deploy the app:
First, we install the Vercel CLI using npm. This tool helps us deploy projects easily. The vercel.json file tells Vercel how to handle the project:
"version": 2 indicates we’re using Vercel’s latest deployment method.
"builds" instructs Vercel to use Python to run manage.py, the Django management script.
"routes" tells Vercel to send all web requests to manage.py so Django can handle routing.
Finally, running vercel in the terminal uploads and deploys the Django project to the cloud. This makes your Django project available online with minimal
configuration.
Hosting Django Application on Render
Instead of setting up servers manually, Render allows you to upload your Django project and it takes care of installing dependencies, running your app, and keeping it
online. This helps beginners deploy applications without worrying about complex server configurations.
Steps to host Django application:
Push your Django project to GitHub.
Go to https://render.com and create an account.
Click on "New Web Service".
Connect your GitHub repository.
Configure the service:
Environment: Python 3
Build Command:
Start Command:
npm i -g vercel
COPY
{
"version": 2,
"builds": [
{ "src": "manage.py", "use": "@vercel/python" }
],
"routes": [
{ "src": "/(.*)", "dest": "manage.py" }
]
}
COPY
vercel
COPY
Render is a cloud platform that makes it easy to deploy web applications, including Django apps, by automating server setup, deployment, and
scaling.
pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY
gunicorn myproject.wsgi
COPY
Click "Create Web Service" and Render will deploy your Django project.
We set the environment to Python 3 because Django runs on Python. The Build Command installs our project’s dependencies listed in requirements.txt. The Start
Command runs the Django app using Gunicorn, a production-grade server, pointing it to our project’s WSGI file. After clicking “Create Web Service”, Render
automatically sets up the server, installs everything, and makes our Django project accessible online.
ASGI
In simple terms, ASGI is like a bridge between your Django application and the server. Unlike WSGI (which only supports synchronous requests), ASGI supports both
synchronous and asynchronous communication. This means Django can handle modern features like WebSockets, real-time updates, and background tasks.
ASGI in Django
By default, Django projects come with an asgi.py file, which acts as the entry point for ASGI servers (like Daphne or Uvicorn). This allows Django to run in
environments where real-time communication is required.
Example: Basic asgi.py in a Django Project
1. import os – This imports the os module to help configure environment variables.
2. from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application – This function creates an ASGI application that Django can use.
3. os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings') – This sets the default settings file for the Django project.
4. application = get_asgi_application() – This creates the ASGI application object that the server (like Uvicorn) will use to serve your Django project.
This file is automatically created when you start a new Django project and is used when deploying the project with an ASGI server.
WSGI
Think of WSGI as a simple contract between your Django app and the web server. The server sends an HTTP request to your app through WSGI, your app processes
it, and WSGI sends the response back. It handles one request at a time per worker (synchronous processing).
WSGI in Django
When deploying a traditional Django site (no WebSockets needed), you run a WSGI server that imports wsgi.py. That file creates a WSGI-compatible application
object. The server uses this object to pass requests to Django and return responses to users.
Example: Basic wsgi.py in a Django Project
ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is a specification that defines how web servers communicate with asynchronous Python web
applications and frameworks, such as Django.
Django uses ASGI to provide asynchronous capabilities, allowing it to handle both traditional HTTP requests and newer protocols like WebSockets.
# asgi.py
import os
from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')
application = get_asgi_application()
COPY
WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) is a Python standard that defines how web servers communicate with Python web applications. It enables
servers and frameworks to work together in a consistent, synchronous way.
Django supports WSGI out of the box and includes a wsgi.py file as the entry point for WSGI servers such as Gunicorn, uWSGI, or mod_wsgi (Apache).
1. import os – Lets the script work with environment variables.
2. from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application – Imports a Django helper that creates a WSGI-compatible application.
3. os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings') – Points Django to your project’s settings.
4. application = get_wsgi_application() – Builds the WSGI application object. Your WSGI server (e.g., Gunicorn) uses this to forward HTTP requests to Django
and return responses to clients.
Nginx
In simple words, Nginx acts as a “middleman” between users and your Django app. When someone visits your site, Nginx receives the request first. If it is for a static
file (like an image or CSS file), Nginx serves it directly. If it is for dynamic content (like Django views), Nginx forwards the request to your Django application server
(like Gunicorn or uWSGI). This makes the website faster and more secure.
Nginx with Django
Django itself is not designed to serve static files in production. Nginx handles those requests quickly and passes only the important application requests to Django.
This setup improves performance, scalability, and security.
Example: Basic Nginx Configuration for Django
1. listen 80; – Nginx listens on port 80 (default HTTP port).
2. server_name example.com; – Defines the domain name of your Django site.
3. location /static/ { alias /home/myproject/static/; } – Tells Nginx to serve static files (CSS, JS, images) directly from the /home/myproject/static/ folder.
4. location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000; } – For all other requests, Nginx forwards them to Django’s application server (e.g., Gunicorn) running on
127.0.0.1:8000.
5. proxy_set_header Host $host; and proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; – Pass important request details (host and client IP) to Django.
This setup ensures Nginx serves static content efficiently and forwards application requests to Django properly.
Environment Variables
Instead of writing sensitive information (like passwords) directly into Django’s code, we use environment variables. This makes applications more secure and easier
to configure across different environments (development, testing, production).
# wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')
application = get_wsgi_application()
COPY

static files and forward requests to application servers.
Nginx is often used with Django in production to serve static files efficiently and to pass dynamic requests to Django’s WSGI/ASGI server.

Environment variables are key-value pairs stored outside the source code, used to configure settings like database credentials, secret keys, or API
tokens in a secure and flexible way.
Example: Using Environment Variables in Django
In the settings.py file, Django imports the os module to read environment variables.
os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY', 'default-secret-key') tries to fetch the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY. If it doesn’t exist, it uses 'default-secret-
key'.
The DEBUG variable is also read from environment variables. Since environment variables are strings, 'True' is compared to set it properly as True
or False.
In the terminal, we set values for DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and DJANGO_DEBUG using the export command.
When Django runs, it picks up these values and uses them instead of hardcoding them inside the code.
Django Admin
Think of Django Admin as a ready-made control panel for your website where you can manage all the data models in your project through a web interface.
Example:
We import admin from django.contrib. We import the Product model created in models.py. We use admin.site.register(Product) to make the Product model
manageable from the admin interface.
Handling Users in Django Admin
Instead of building your own user management system, Django gives you a simple interface where you can manage users directly.
Example:
# settings.py
import os
# Get secret key from environment variable
SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY', 'default-secret-key')
# Get debug mode setting from environment variable
DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', 'False') == 'True'
COPY
# In your terminal or .env file
export DJANGO_SECRET_KEY='my-secret-key-123'
export DJANGO_DEBUG='True'
COPY
Django Admin is a built-in web interface in Django that helps you manage your website’s data. It allows you to add, edit, view, and delete database
records without writing any code.
# In admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Product
admin.site.register(Product)
COPY
Django Admin provides a default interface to manage user accounts. You can create, update, or delete users and manage their passwords from the
admin panel.
- Visit http://localhost:8000/admin/
- Log in with a superuser account.
- Go to the "Users" section.
- Add a new user by filling out username, password, and email.
COPY
Open the admin interface in your browser. Log in with your superuser credentials. Under Users, you can manage users. Click Add user, enter details, and save the
user record.
Permissions in Django Admin
You can limit users so they only see or change what they’re allowed to, which helps keep your site safe and organized.
Example:
Groups in Django Admin
Instead of assigning permissions to every user one by one, you can group users (like "Editors", "Moderators") and manage permissions for the group.
Example:
When you assign a user to this group, they inherit all group permissions.
CRUD in Django Admin
You don’t need to write code for basic database operations. Django Admin provides easy forms and lists to manage your data records.
Example:
1. Create: Open the admin, click "Add Product", fill in product details, and save.
2. Read: Products are listed in a table in the admin interface.
3. Update: Click a product name, modify fields, and save.\
4. Delete: Select a product and click "Delete" to remove it from the database.

- Assign “Can add product” and “Can change product” permissions to the group.
